questions.text:
For two different persons [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex], the predicate [latex]M(x, y)[/latex] denotes that [latex]x[/latex] knows [latex]y[/latex].
Consider the following statement.

There is a person who does not know anyone else, but that person is known by everyone else.

Which one of the following expressions represents the above statement?
questions.solution:
We need to translate: "There is a person [latex]y[/latex] such that [latex]y[/latex] doesn't know anyone else, but everyone else knows [latex]y[/latex]."

- "There is a person [latex]y[/latex]" → [latex](\exists y)[/latex].
- "for every other person [latex]x[/latex] ([latex]x\ne y[/latex])" → [latex](\forall x)(x\ne y\rightarrow\ldots)[/latex].
- "[latex]x[/latex] knows [latex]y[/latex]" (everyone else knows this person) → [latex]M(x,y)[/latex].
- "[latex]y[/latex] does not know [latex]x[/latex]" (this person doesn't know anyone else) → [latex]\neg M(y,x)[/latex].

Combining: [latex](\exists y)(\forall x)\big((x\ne y)\rightarrow(M(x,y)\wedge\neg M(y,x))\big)[/latex] — there exists such a special person [latex]y[/latex], and for every other person [latex]x[/latex], [latex]x[/latex] knows [latex]y[/latex] but [latex]y[/latex] does not know [latex]x[/latex].

The other options either use [latex]\forall y[/latex] (wrongly requiring every person to have this property, instead of just one special person), or use [latex]\exists x[/latex] (existentially quantifying [latex]x[/latex] instead of requiring it for every other person), which don't match the intended meaning.

Answer: [latex](\exists y)(\forall x)\left((x\neq y)\rightarrow(M(x,y)\wedge\neg M(y,x))\right)[/latex]

Click here for detail solution
options: [latex](\exists y)(\forall x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))[/latex]
[latex](\forall y)(\exists x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))[/latex]
[latex](\exists y)(\exists x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))[/latex]
[latex](\forall y)(\forall x)((x \neq y) \rightarrow(M(x, y) \wedge \neg M(y, x)))[/latex]

questions.text:
The set [latex]\mathbf{T}[/latex] represents various traversals over binary tree. The set [latex]\mathbf{S}[/latex] represents the order of visiting nodes during a traversal.

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \quad\quad\textbf{T} & \quad\quad\quad\textbf{S} \\ \hline \text{I: Inorder} & \text{L: left subtree, node, right subtree} \\ \text{II: Preorder} & \text{M: node, left subtree, right subtree} \\ \text{III: Postorder} & \text{N: left subtree, right subtree, node} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

Which one of the following is the correct match from [latex]\mathbf{T}[/latex] to [latex]\mathbf{S}[/latex] ?
questions.solution:
Recall the definitions of each traversal (in terms of the order root/current node is visited relative to its subtrees):

- Inorder (I): visit left subtree, then the node itself, then right subtree — this matches L (left subtree, node, right subtree).
- Preorder (II): visit the node itself first, then left subtree, then right subtree — this matches M (node, left subtree, right subtree).
- Postorder (III): visit left subtree, then right subtree, and the node itself last — this matches N (left subtree, right subtree, node).

Answer: I-L, II-M, III-N

questions.text:
Which one of the following statements is equivalent to the following assertion?

Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] decides the language [latex]L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*[/latex]
questions.solution:
A Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] "decides" a language [latex]L[/latex] means [latex]M[/latex] is a total decider for [latex]L[/latex]: it must halt on every input, and its halting outcome must correctly classify membership — accepting every string that is in [latex]L[/latex], and rejecting every string that is not in [latex]L[/latex] (i.e. every string in [latex]\{0,1\}^*-L[/latex]).

Simply halting on all inputs (without specifying correct accept/reject behavior) isn't enough by itself, and neither "accepts all of [latex]L[/latex]" nor "rejects all of the complement" alone captures the full requirement (each addresses only one direction). Only the combination of both conditions together is equivalent to "decides [latex]L[/latex]."

Answer: M accepts all strings in L and rejects all strings in {0,1}*-L

Click here for detail solution
options: Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] halts on all input strings in [latex]\{0,1\}^{*}[/latex]
Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] accepts all input strings in [latex]L[/latex]
Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] rejects all input strings in [latex]\{0,1\}^{*}-L[/latex]
Turing machine [latex]M[/latex] accepts all input strings in [latex]L[/latex] and rejects all input strings in [latex]\{0,1\}^{*}-L[/latex]

questions.text:
The probability density function [latex]f(x)[/latex] of a random variable [latex]X[/latex] which takes real values is

[latex] f(x)=\frac{1}{3 \sqrt{2 \pi}} \exp \left(-\frac{x^{2}}{18}\right), \quad x \in(-\infty,+\infty) [/latex]

Which one of the following statements is correct about the random variable [latex]X[/latex] ?
questions.solution:
The given density [latex]f(x)=\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\dfrac{x^2}{18}\right)[/latex] has exactly the form of the Gaussian/normal density [latex]f(x)=\dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\dfrac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)[/latex] with mean [latex]\mu=0[/latex] and, matching [latex]2\sigma^2=18\Rightarrow\sigma^2=9\Rightarrow\sigma=3[/latex] (consistent with the [latex]\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{2\pi}}[/latex] normalizing constant).

This is the defining bell-curve density of a normal (Gaussian) random variable with mean [latex]0[/latex] and standard deviation [latex]3[/latex] — it doesn't match the forms of an exponential, Poisson (which is discrete, not even a continuous density), or uniform distribution.

Answer: X is a normal random variable

questions.text:
In the context of DBMS, consider the two sets [latex]\mathbf{T}[/latex] and [latex]\mathbf{S}[/latex] given below.

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \quad\quad\quad\textbf{T} & \quad\quad\quad\textbf{S} \\ \hline \text{I: Logical schema} & \text{L: Views} \\ \text{II: Physical schema} & \text{M: File organization and indexes} \\ \text{III: External schema} & \text{N: Relations} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

Which one of the following is the correct match from [latex]\mathbf{T}[/latex] to [latex]\mathbf{S}[/latex] ?
questions.solution:
Matching each schema level in the three-tier DBMS architecture to what it describes:

- Logical schema (I): describes the overall logical structure of the database for the whole community of users — this is exactly what relations (N) capture.
- Physical schema (II): describes how data is actually stored at the lowest level — file organization and indexes (M).
- External schema (III): describes a customized, user-specific way of seeing part of the data — exactly what views (L) provide.

Answer: I-N, II-M, III-L
